title: ATV offers to buy Dick James’s Northern Songs shares | 1969
content:
On 28 March 1969 Associated Television (ATV), a media company run by Lew Grade, made an offer to buy music publisher Dick James and his lawyer Charles Silver’s shares in The Beatles’ publishing company Northern Songs.

James and Silver had held a 32% stake in the company since its floatation on the London Stock Exchange in February 1965. However, since the death of Beatles manager Brian Epstein in August 1967, James predicted that the group’s days were numbered, and sought to sever ties before the Northern Songs share price declined.

On this day Grade offered James and Silver 37 shillings per share – for a total of £1,525,000. The following day Grade told The Times that the deal was “brewed up by both sets of directors over a cup of coffee last Monday.”

ATV already owned 137,000 shares in Northern Songs. With the additional 1,604,750 shares, ATV would secure almost 35% of Northern Songs. The offer was made formally on 11 April.

James failed to give John Lennon and Paul McCartney the option to buy the shares, and waited to meet Grade until they were both out of the country. He also failed to notify Northern Songs’ other major shareholder, NEMS Enterprises.

James later said he conducted the business in this way to avoid press leaks. “What I did, I did in their interests as well as mine, and the rest of the shareholders. I was not acting behind their backs. I believed I was acting for them and for the whole future good of the company.”

The prospect of a Northern Songs takeover led to heightened speculation, and various offers and counter-offers, culminating in The Beatles’ loss of the company in September 1969.
